title: Bloom filter for joins with one equality key plus non-equality conditions
hypothesis: In q21, the two subquery joins `lineitem l2/l3 ⋈ DELIM_SCAN ON l_orderkey = l_orderkey AND l_suppkey != l_suppkey` (profile: HASH_JOIN 1.10s producing 1.85M rows, plus the sibling join producing 2.93M rows) probe the whole lineitem table against a build side of about 708K distinct (orderkey, suppkey) pairs. No bloom filter gets pushed into the lineitem scan. The reason is in `JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter` (`src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp`:775), which requires `ht->conditions.size() == 1`, and these joins have two conditions. The join hash table only hashes the equality columns (`equality_predicate_columns`, join_hashtable.cpp:43-60), and `InsertHashes` feeds those same hashes into the bloom filter (join_hashtable.cpp:720). So with exactly one equality condition, the filter is a valid membership test on that key alone, whatever non-equality conditions are also present. A second gate also blocks it: when the build side is a `LOGICAL_DELIM_GET`, `build_side_has_filter` is computed as `IsFiltering(join.children[0])`, i.e. on the probe side (join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:304-305). The l2 lineitem scan has no filter, so its join never gets a bloom filter. A delim build side is a de-duplicated set of keys from the outer query. Here it covers about 5% of order keys, so a bloom filter would cut about 60M probe rows to about 3M per subquery scan.
plan: 1) In `CanUseBloomFilter` (physical_hash_join.cpp ~775), replace `ht->conditions.size() == 1` with `ht->equality_predicate_columns.size() == 1` (or count the conditions that are COMPARE_EQUAL / NOT_DISTINCT_FROM), keeping `cmp == COMPARE_EQUAL`. Check that the filter column / condition index pushed is the equality one (conditions are reordered so equalities come first, `ReorderConditions` in `GenerateJoinFilters`), and that `PushBloomFilter`'s use of `ht.conditions[0]` and `NullValuesAreEqual(0)` points at that equality condition. 2) In `JoinFilterPushdownOptimizer::GenerateJoinFilters` (join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:303-308), when the rhs is a `LOGICAL_DELIM_GET`, set `build_side_has_filter = true`, or `IsFiltering(children[0]) || <the delim side is a distinct set>`. The existing `probe_larger_then_build` check (estimated probe cardinality > HT count) still prevents wasted builds. Make sure min/max filters for non-equality conditions behave as before. Run `bench q21` and check in `profile` that the lineitem scans under the delim joins show `BF(l_orderkey)` and far fewer rows.
expected_gain: q21: the two lineitem subquery scans and their probes (about 1.1s + ~0.5s operator time) should shrink sharply. I expect 20-40% lower latency.
generality: Helps any hash join with one equality key plus extra inequality/range conditions (common in rewritten correlated EXISTS/NOT EXISTS subqueries, e.g. TPC-H q21/q22-like and other correlated subqueries with residual predicates), and any correlated subquery decorrelated into a join with a DELIM_GET build side over an unfiltered probe table. It could be slightly slower where the bloom filter rejects little, but the existing SelectivityOptionalFilter turns the filter off adaptively when it doesn't help, and the probe>build check still applies.
risk: Low-medium. Correctness depends on the bloom filter hashing exactly the single equality key in the same way as `BFTableFilter::HashInternal` (both use VectorOperations::Hash on one column). With NOT DISTINCT FROM as the only equality, cmp != EQUAL keeps it excluded. Any mismatch in condition index → wrong results, so verify on queries with mixed conditions.

title: Bloom filter for sparse perfect-hash joins
hypothesis: The main chain of q21 accounts for most of its time. Run alone without the subqueries, it takes 0.658s wall of the 0.835s query. In that chain, the lineitem l1 scan has no selective filter: FILTER (l_receiptdate>l_commitdate) emits 37.9M rows and the INNER join l_suppkey=s_suppkey (0.38s CPU) cuts them to 1.52M. The build side is supplier⋈nation with 4,009 keys spread over a key range of about 100K. That fits a perfect hash table (range <= 1M, physical_hash_join.cpp Finalize -> CanDoPerfectHashJoin). JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:769) returns false for any perfect hash table, on the reasoning that 'we expect good min/max pruning'. With 4% density spread over the whole range, min/max prunes nothing, so the probe-side scan decodes all its columns for all 60M rows. A 4-column lineitem scan measured 2.2-3.4s CPU, while a 2-column scan measured about 1.0s. A bloom filter on l_suppkey in the scan would drop about 96% of rows before the other columns are fetched (the scan fetches non-filter columns only for selected rows) and before the FILTER and the join probe run.
plan: 1) In CanUseBloomFilter (src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp ~761), replace the unconditional `if (is_perfect_hashtable) return false;` with a density check. Allow the bloom filter for a perfect hash table only if the build is sparse: ht->Count() * 4 < build_range + 1, where build_range is the perfect_join_statistics.build_range that CanDoPerfectHashJoin has computed. Pass the range (or a bool `perfect_ht_is_sparse`) from PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize to FinalizeFilters and on to CanUseBloomFilter. All other conditions stay: build_side_has_filter, probe estimate > build count, single EQUAL condition, no cast. 2) The bloom filter is filled during the regular finalize (JoinHashTable::Finalize initialises it when should_build_bloom_filter is set; InsertHashes fills it; HashJoinFinalizeEvent::FinishEvent pushes the deferred filters). The perfect path skips ScheduleFinalize (Finalize ~1017), so when use_perfect_hash is set and sink.deferred_bloom_filters is not empty, still call sink.ScheduleFinalize(pipeline, event). Keep perfect_join_executor so the probe still uses the perfect hash table. Building the pointer table for a small build (<=256K rows when sparse) is cheap. Check that BuildPerfectHashTable does not consume the data collection; it only scans it. If finalizing alongside the perfect hash table proves unsafe, fall back to this: when the build is sparse and a bloom filter is deferred, set use_perfect_hash=false (reset the executor and take the normal path). 3) Confirm with `dbe-tool sql "EXPLAIN ANALYZE <main chain of q21>"` that the lineitem scan shows `l_suppkey IN BF` and that the FILTER above it gets far fewer than 37.9M rows.
expected_gain: q21: -15..-30%. The l1 lineitem scan should drop from about 2-3s CPU to under 1s, FILTER from 60M to about 2.4M rows, and the suppkey join probe from 37.9M to about 1.5M rows.
generality: Helps any star or snowflake join where a filtered dimension with dense integer keys (a perfect-hash candidate) is joined to a large fact table: dimension filters like nation/region/category on TPC-H/SSB/TPC-DS. Today those joins never get a bloom filter. Could be slower: queries where the build keys are sparse but nearly every probe value matches, so the bloom filter filters nothing. SelectivityOptionalFilter (BF_THRESHOLD) turns itself off after its check window, so the cost is bounded to a short trial plus building the pointer table and bloom filter for the small build.
risk: Medium-low. Main correctness risk is running the regular finalize alongside the perfect hash table (finalized flag, pinned data collection). The fallback (dropping the perfect hash table when sparse) is trivially correct. Bloom filters are optional filters, so the results do not depend on them.

title: Join filters for RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI probe sides incl. DELIM_GET builds
hypothesis: In q21 both decorrelated subqueries probe a full 60M-row lineitem scan against a small delim key set (708K distinct (orderkey,suppkey) of 15M orders). BuildProbeSideOptimizer (optimizer.cpp:247) runs before JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN (optimizer.cpp:320), so the EXISTS-side inner join is already flipped SEMI->RIGHT_SEMI (probe=lineitem l2, build=DELIM_GET) and GenerateJoinFilters (join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:210-219) returns early for RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI -> no min/max or BF reaches the l2 scan; all 60M rows are hashed and probed (2.93M survive). Even where filters are generated, build_side_has_filter for a DELIM_GET rhs is computed on children[0] (the probe, unfiltered lineitem) -> false -> no BF; and CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:775) requires ht->conditions.size()==1 although these joins have 'l_orderkey = ... AND l_suppkey <> ...'. E0001 fixed the last two and the NOT EXISTS join dropped 0.92s->0.31s CPU, but the EXISTS (RIGHT_SEMI) side was untouched because of the early return. For RIGHT_SEMI and RIGHT_ANTI, probe rows without a build match never influence the output (only build rows are emitted, match flags are only set by matching probe rows), so filtering the probe side by the build key set is exactly as safe as for INNER/SEMI. The FIXME about inverting conditions applies to ANTI (probe-preserving), not RIGHT_ANTI.
plan: 1) src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp GenerateJoinFilters: remove JoinType::RIGHT_SEMI and JoinType::RIGHT_ANTI from the early-return switch (keep LEFT/OUTER/ANTI/MARK/SINGLE), with a comment why it is safe. 2) Same file ~line 304: when rhs_child is LOGICAL_DELIM_GET set build_side_has_filter = true (a delim get is the deduplicated key set of the outer side, which is by construction a subset of the probe keys and is typically far smaller; the existing probe-est > HT-count check in CanUseBloomFilter still guards). 3) src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter: replace ht->conditions.size()==1 with ht->equality_predicate_columns.size()==1 (equalities come first; BF hashes only equality cols; non-equality conds still fail the cmp==COMPARE_EQUAL check). Verify PushBloomFilter uses conditions[0] / NullValuesAreEqual(0). Verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that both l2 and l3 lineitem scans show 'l_orderkey IN BF(...)' and their row counts drop to a few M; run full bench result checks. If the RIGHT_SEMI physical path in join_hashtable.cpp (lines ~994-1030, 1406-1436) makes any assumption about probe rows count, check it.
expected_gain: q21 -8..-15% (E0001 alone gave -3.8..-7.5% from the NOT EXISTS side; the EXISTS side probes the same 60M rows against the same-size key set, so roughly doubles the saving).
generality: Any EXISTS/IN/NOT EXISTS subquery that the planner flips to RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI (small outer key set, big inner table) — common in TPC-H q4/q20/q21/q22-style and decorrelated correlated subqueries with extra non-equality predicates. Could be slightly slower when the build key set covers most probe keys (BF hashing overhead ~7ns/row with no rejection); existing probe>build cardinality gate limits this.
risk: Low-medium. Correctness: RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI semantics only depend on matching probe rows, so dropping non-matching probe rows is safe; NULL keys handled by existing filters_null_values logic. Perf risk: BF probe cost on probe sides with little rejection.

title: Bloom filter probe: hash+lookup only run heads of equal consecutive keys
hypothesis: Warm profile of q21 (3rd run in the same process, JSON profiling): the l2 and l3 lineitem scans carry `optional: l_orderkey IN BF(l_orderkey)` and cost 0.72s and 0.86s CPU for 60M rows each. A plain warm 2-column scan of the same columns costs 0.18s CPU, and hashing 60M BIGINTs costs about 0.15s (EXPLAIN ANALYZE bit_xor(hash(l_orderkey))). So about 0.4-0.5s per scan is hashing plus random BF lookups: 708K keys give a 2MB filter, which misses L2. That is about 1.2s of the query's ~4.7s CPU. lineitem is clustered on the join key (about 4 consecutive rows per key), so most hash/lookup work repeats the previous row's. If BFTableFilter::Filter checks whether key[i]==key[i-1] and reuses the previous result, hashing and lookups drop about 4x on clustered data.
plan: In src/planner/filter/bloom_filter.cpp, BFTableFilter::Filter: add a fast path when keys_v is a FLAT_VECTOR, its physical type is a fixed-width integer (INT8..INT64, UINT8..UINT64; a template over T), and it has no NULLs in the approved rows (validity AllValid, or a cheap per-row check). Steps: (1) walk the approved rows (through sel if set, otherwise 0..count-1) and write the positions where key != previous approved key into a head selection (state.bf_sel or a new buffer in BFTableFilterState, src/include/duckdb/planner/table_filter_state.hpp). (2) If heads > ~3/4 of approved_tuple_count, fall back to the existing path, so unclustered data pays only one compare per row. (3) Otherwise slice keys_v by the head sel, run VectorOperations::Hash on the heads only, and call filter.LookupOne per head (or LookupHashes). (4) Walk the approved rows again, carrying the current head's found flag, and compact sel / approved_tuple_count the way the current code does (keep the existing semantics: sel.Initialize(bf_sel) when sel was not set, otherwise remap). Results are identical to the per-row path because equal keys hash identically. Do not touch BloomFilter itself.
expected_gain: q21: l2+l3 scans 1.58s → ~0.8s CPU, out of ~4.7s total CPU. Roughly -8..-15% wall. Also l1-type scans if a BF is ever pushed on a clustered key.
generality: Helps any join-filter BF probe on a column stored clustered or sorted by the join key, which is common for fact tables loaded in key order (lineitem/orders, events by id, time-sorted data): semi joins, delim joins, FK joins with selective build sides. Unclustered columns pay one extra compare per row plus the fallback check, under 0.5ns/row.
risk: Low. Results are unchanged by construction. The main correctness hazards are NULL handling (fall back when any NULL is present) and sel remapping. Edge risk: the adaptive fallback threshold is wrong for data that alternates between clustered and not, costing a small amount of extra work.

title: Cheap run-deduped BF probe + push BF into DELIM_GET-build subquery scans
hypothesis: In a warm JSON profile of the current best q21 (latency 1.03s, ~7s summed CPU, so the query is CPU-bound), the two subquery INNER hash joins (lineitem probe ⋈ DELIM_SCAN build on l_orderkey = AND l_suppkey <>) are the two largest operators: l2 join 1.79s CPU over 59.99M probe rows (2.93M matches), l3 join 1.09s over 37.9M rows (1.85M matches). Their scans carry only useless min/max filters (5..59999777). E0003 pushed a BF into both scans: scan output fell to ~3.5M rows and the join to ~0.44s, but the scans' CPU rose by 0.6-0.9s each (hash + random 64-bit-sector lookup on every row), which cancelled the gain. E0004 wrote a fast path in BFTableFilter::Filter for flat, NULL-free integer keys: it hashes inline and reuses the previous result while the key equals the previous key. It had no target because no BF reached clustered keys. Together the two should work: probe keys come in runs (the table is clustered on the join key, ~4 rows per key), so the fast path removes most of the per-row hash and lookup. That leaves the join savings (~2s CPU) while cutting the scan penalty (~1.5s) by a factor of 3-4.
plan: Three parts in one diff. (1) src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp GenerateJoinFilters, around lines 302-309: when join.children[1] is LOGICAL_DELIM_GET, set build_side_has_filter = true. A DELIM_GET carries the distinct keys of an already-filtered outer side. Keep the existing probe > build cardinality check. (2) src/execution/operator/join/physical_hash_join.cpp JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (line ~775): replace `ht->conditions.size() == 1` with `ht->equality_predicate_columns.size() == 1` and keep the `cmp == COMPARE_EQUAL` requirement. Equalities are ordered first, so conditions[0] is the equality that PushBloomFilter uses. (3) src/planner/filter/bloom_filter.cpp BFTableFilter::Filter: add a fast path when keys_v is FLAT, has no NULLs in the approved rows, and has an integer physical type (INT8..INT64, UINT8..UINT64). Walk the approved rows (through sel if set). Keep prev_key and prev_found. When key != prev_key, compute duckdb::Hash<T>(key), the same function VectorOperations::Hash uses, and call filter.LookupOne. Write survivors directly into sel and approved_tuple_count. Any other input uses the existing path. Check with a JSON profile that both l2 and l3 scans show `IN BF(l_orderkey)` and that scan CPU stays under ~0.5s each.
expected_gain: q21: -8% to -15%. Join CPU falls by ~2s, scan CPU rises by ~0.4s instead of ~1.5s, out of ~7s total CPU.
generality: Any correlated EXISTS/NOT EXISTS or IN subquery that is decorrelated into a delim join whose inner side scans a large table on the correlation key. Also any hash join with one equality plus residual non-equality conditions. The fast path helps every BF probe on integer keys that come in sorted or clustered runs (fact tables ordered by a foreign key). It could get slower: BF probes on unique or random integer keys pay one extra compare per row (negligible), and DELIM_GET builds that filter nothing get a BF they don't need. The probe > build cardinality gate limits that case.
risk: Low to medium. Correctness: the BF is optional, and for NULL-free integer keys the inline hash must match VectorOperations::Hash exactly, so use duckdb::Hash<T>. Fall back for any vector with NULLs or that is not flat. Performance risk: the gain may still be under the 5% bar, since parts 1-2 alone gave 0%.

title: Hash join probe: reuse hash/bucket for consecutive equal integer probe keys
hypothesis: If the BF route fails: the l2 and l3 subquery joins spend ~30ns per probe row (1.79s / 60M rows) on a 735K-entry pointer table that does not fit in cache. Probe keys come in runs of ~4 equal values, so 3/4 of the hashes and pointer-table misses repeat the previous row's work.
plan: In JoinHashTable probe (src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp, the hash and GetRowPointers path), for a single flat, NULL-free integer key column, compute the hash once per run and copy the bucket pointer or salt result to the following equal keys. Verify the function names before implementing.
expected_gain: q21: -5% to -10%, if the probe is dominated by cache misses on the pointer table.
generality: Hash joins probed by clustered or sorted foreign keys. Unique or random keys pay one compare per row.
risk: Medium. The probe code is intricate: salts, chains, and residual non-equality predicates.

title: Exact key-bitmap mode for join BF + push BF into DELIM_GET-build subquery scans
hypothesis: E0005 pushed a BF into the q21 l2/l3 lineitem scans. That cut join CPU by 2.2s (l2 1.79→0.39s, l3 1.09→0.31s), but the BF added about 0.7s of scan CPU (l2 0.33→0.62s, l3 0.35→0.77s), even with run-dedupe. The net was -4%, just under the 5% bar. Reading ProbeForPointersInternal (join_hashtable.cpp:188) explains the l2/l3 join cost: about 56M of the 60M probe rows miss, and each miss is a hash plus one random load into a pointer table of several MB. With keys clustered about 4 per run, that is about 15M distinct cache misses per join. The BF has the same problem: it is hashed, so the accesses are random. When the build key is an integer with a range (max-min+1) of at most about 64x the build count, an exact bitmap indexed by key-min replaces hash+sector-lookup with a subtract, a shift and a bit test. For sorted or clustered probe keys the bitmap is read sequentially, which costs almost nothing. It is also exact, so the joins receive only the 3.5M real matches. This should keep most of E0005's 2.2s join saving and remove most of its 0.7s scan overhead.
plan: (a) Re-apply E0005 parts 1+2. In join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp GenerateJoinFilters, set build_side_has_filter=true when the build child is LOGICAL_DELIM_GET. In physical_hash_join.cpp CanUseBloomFilter (:761), replace `ht->conditions.size()==1` with `ht->equality_predicate_columns.size()==1`, still requiring cmp==COMPARE_EQUAL. (b) In BloomFilter (src/planner/filter/bloom_filter.cpp + its header), add an optional exact-bitmap mode: `int64 bitmap_min`, a bit count, and an atomic<uint64_t> array. Initialize it in JoinHashTable::AllocatePointerTable (join_hashtable.cpp:741), or at the point where the build key min/max is known (finalize of build stats in PhysicalHashJoin::Finalize, the same min/max used for the min/max filters). Conditions: the key is a single integral type (INT8..INT64/UINT8..UINT32), min/max are known, and range+1 <= 64*Count() and <= 2^29 bits. Otherwise keep the normal BF. Fill the bitmap from the build key values in parallel in HashJoinFinalizeTask: gather the key column from the data collection chunks it already iterates, then fetch_or the bits, skipping NULLs. If the keys are not easily reachable there, build it in InsertHashes' caller from the key vector. (c) In BFTableFilter::Filter (:96), if bitmap mode is on and the vector is integral: for each approved row, keep it iff the key is in [min,max] and bit(key-min) is set. Preserve the existing NULL handling (filters_null_values). Write survivors into sel/approved_tuple_count exactly like the existing path. Make FilterValue and CheckStatistics (:135/:173) bitmap-aware or leave them conservative (CheckStatistics can always return NO_PRUNING_POSSIBLE in bitmap mode). Leave Serialize untouched. Verify with the warm JSON-profile recipe in memory that the l2/l3 scans show `IN BF(` and emit about 3.5M rows, and that the scan CPU is close to 0.35s.
expected_gain: q21: -7% to -15%. E0005's -4% plus most of the 0.7s scan-side BF overhead removed, and joins get exact (not probabilistic) filtering. The orders-scan BF (o_orderkey, dense range) also gets the cheaper bitmap.
generality: Any hash join on integer keys whose build key range is dense relative to the build count, which is typical for surrogate/foreign keys (star and snowflake joins, EXISTS/IN subqueries on keys). The bitmap is exact and branch-cheap even for random probe order. Sparse ranges fall back to the existing BF. Possible slowdowns: very large bitmaps (capped), and the extra build-time pass over the keys for small probe sides (BF is already gated on probe > build).
risk: Medium. The bitmap must be fully populated before the filter is visible, so reuse the existing deferred_bloom_filters / FinishEvent path. Signed range arithmetic needs care (use uint64 of key-min after the range check). NULL semantics must match the BF path. E0005 parts were already validated correct on hidden queries.
